hints.title: Separate input changes from height changes
hints.body: For each transformation, write which height of the original graph corresponds to a zero of the new function. An input translation or reflection rearranges horizontal positions; an added constant changes the required height.
hints.recap: Root counts after a transformation can be read as horizontal-line intersections.
hints.pitfall: A vertical translation need not preserve the number of roots.
hints.pause: Translate all three root questions into statements about the original graph.

recall.reminder: Root counts after a transformation can be read as horizontal-line intersections.

hints.title: Locate the turning heights
hints.body: Differentiate the cubic, factor its derivative and find both stationary inputs. Substitute them into the original function. Use the fact that the original cubic has three distinct roots.
hints.recap: The two turning heights determine which horizontal lines meet a cubic three times.
hints.pitfall: A horizontal line through a turning point gives a repeated root, so distinctness requires care.
hints.pause: Identify the local maximum and minimum and locate the target horizontal levels relative to them.

recall.reminder: The two turning heights determine which horizontal lines meet a cubic three times.

hints.title: Test a claim that is not forced
hints.body: If a target level is not guaranteed to lie between the turning heights, choose an allowed parameter placing a turning height on the other side of that level. Verify that the original still has three distinct roots.
hints.recap: A counterexample must retain every original assumption.
hints.pitfall: One favourable sketch cannot prove that a transformation always works.
hints.pause: Complete the guaranteed cases and verify an explicit counterexample for any remaining case.

recall.reminder: A counterexample must retain every original assumption.

solution:
Let f(x)=x3+3qx2+2. Its derivative is f′(x)=3x(x+2q), so its stationary heights are f(0)=2 and f(−2q)=2+4q3. Three distinct roots require a local maximum above zero and a local minimum below zero. Thus q<0 and 2+4q3<0; the maximum is 2 and the minimum is 2+4q3.

For I, f(x)+1=0 asks for intersections of f with height −1. The minimum need not be below −1: take q=−45, giving minimum −6125. The original has three roots, but after adding 1 both turning heights are positive, leaving only one root. I is not guaranteed.

For II, f(x+1)=0 simply translates each original root one unit left. The three roots remain distinct.

For III, f(−x)−1=0 means f(−x)=1. The height 1 is strictly between the minimum (which is negative) and the maximum 2, so there are three intersections. Reflection changes their positions without merging them. II and III are guaranteed. Answer G.
knowledgePattern: Use cubic turning heights to test which transformations preserve three roots
